content.text: Clauses 18.1 to 18.4 (framework comparison, domain and category structure, the standards crosswalk, and the evidence index) and clauses 18.5 to 18.11 (the self-study process, stakeholder involvement, visit preparation, mini self-reviews, action plans, evidence and artifacts, and roles and responsibilities) are all written. Clauses 18.5 to 18.11 were authored by Eduversal on 2026-08-17 and are new content rather than transcribed source material; each carries its own provenance note. Their procedural facts are cited inline to ACS WASC Focus on Learning (2019 edition) and to the CIS Evaluation Framework [Revised] and CIS Instructions for Submission (August 2024), with page numbers, so any statement can be checked at source. Where CIS and ACS WASC differ, both are stated separately rather than merged into a single false process. Two source cautions worth carrying into any review of this section: WASC Focus on Learning 2020 is the Supplementary Education Programs edition and is NOT authority for whole-school accreditation (use the 2019 edition), and two CIS frameworks are currently in circulation - see 18.2.

International accreditation through the Council of International Schools (CIS) and the Western Association of Schools and Colleges (WASC) represents more than a certificate on the wall—it is a comprehensive quality assurance framework that validates our commitment to continuous improvement and educational excellence. For Eduversal Partner Schools, pursuing CIS and WASC accreditation aligns directly with our mission to provide world-class Cambridge education integrated with Indonesian values and compliance requirements.
content.title: Purpose of International Accreditation
Why Pursue International Accreditation?
steps: Quality Assurance and Validation International accreditation provides external validation that our school meets rigorous global standards for educational excellence. It assures parents, students, university admissions officers, and other stakeholders that we deliver high-quality education comparable to the world's best international schools.

Continuous Improvement Culture Accreditation is not a one-time achievement but an ongoing cycle of self-reflection, evidence collection, stakeholder feedback, and systematic improvement. It transforms quality assurance from compliance-driven to values-driven practice.

International Recognition CIS and WASC accreditation is recognized worldwide by universities, educational authorities, and international school networks. It enhances student mobility and university admissions prospects, particularly for students applying to institutions in North America, Europe, and other regions that value these credentials.

Stakeholder Confidence Accreditation demonstrates to the Yayasan (Foundation), parents, prospective families, and the wider community that the school is committed to accountability, transparency, and evidence-based decision-making.

Professional Development and Networking The accreditation process connects our schools to a global community of educators committed to excellence. It provides access to professional development opportunities, peer schools for collaboration, and best practices from around the world.
Alignment with Eduversal's Commitment to Excellence Accreditation aligns seamlessly with Eduversal's Quality Management System, including:

items: EASE (Eduversal Analytical & Skills Evaluation) for internal benchmarking
EduNav platform for evidence repository and dashboards
DTP (Development of Teaching Proficiency) for professional growth
Appraisal Program for teacher and school evaluation

content.text: Many schools approach accreditation as a compliance exercise—a massive documentation effort undertaken months before the accreditation visit, followed by relief when the team departs. This approach is exhausting, unsustainable, and misses the true value of accreditation. At Eduversal Partner Schools, we embed accreditation into our daily operations. Evidence collection, stakeholder feedback, and continuous improvement are not special projects—they are how we work. This approach means: Daily Practice Becomes Evidence When teachers maintain well-organized lesson plans, conduct moderation sessions, and track student progress systematically, they are simultaneously fulfilling their professional responsibilities and generating accreditation evidence. Strategic Planning Drives Improvement Our School Improvement Plan (SIP) and Strategic Plan (see Section 4) are not separate from accreditation action plans—they are the same documents, ensuring our improvement efforts are coherent and sustained. Stakeholder Engagement Is Ongoing Rather than scrambling to survey parents and students before an accreditation visit, we conduct regular stakeholder feedback as part of our quality assurance cycle (see Sections 16 and 17), making accreditation simply a validation of existing practices. Leadership Monitors Progress Continuously Through EduNav dashboards and termly mini self-reviews (see Section 18.8), school leadership has real-time visibility into accreditation readiness, allowing course corrections long before external reviewers arrive.
content.title: Accreditation as Embedded Practice vs. One-Time Event

content.text: ACS WASC operates a six-year accreditation cycle, with a mid-cycle visit before the end of the third year. The CIS International Accreditation Evaluation Framework [Revised] describes a five-year cycle: its team-evaluation criteria are the ones that "support school improvement throughout the five-year cycle." Plan against five years, but confirm the dates with CIS before committing, because CIS is changing its framework - see the note in Section 18.2. However, schools should begin preparation at least 12-18 months before formal self-study begins to ensure systems, evidence, and stakeholder engagement mechanisms are firmly in place. Typical Accreditation Timeline: YEAR 1 (Pre-Self-Study Phase)

items: Months 1-6: Decision to pursue accreditation; initial application to CIS/WASC; assign Accreditation Coordinator; conduct preliminary evidence audit
Months 7-12: Establish continuous evidence collection systems in EduNav; conduct baseline stakeholder surveys; initiate termly mini self-reviews

content.title: Indonesian recognition of international accreditation bodies
items: Kepmendikdasmen No. 73/O/2025, dated 3 June 2025, lists the international accreditation bodies recognised by the Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education.

The recognised bodies are: ACS-WASC (Accrediting Commission for Schools - Western Association of Schools and Colleges); CIS (Council of International Schools); ASIC (Accreditation Service for International Colleges); and ACSI (Association of Christian Schools International).

Diktum KEDUA of the decree states that these are "Lembaga Akreditasi Internasional yang diakui oleh Kementerian Pendidikan Dasar dan Menengah" - international accreditation bodies recognised by the Ministry.

This matters for two reasons. It confirms that a CIS or ACS-WASC accreditation is recognised by the Indonesian Ministry, and it means a school choosing an accreditor outside this list carries the burden of showing recognition separately.
National accreditation through BAN-S/M is a separate obligation and is not replaced by international accreditation.

Source: Permendikdasmen No. 73/2025, salinan at Desktop/Eduversal Sources/mevzuat/Nomor 73 Tahun 2025.pdf (not yet extracted into docs/research/ — this is a pointer to the source document, not an archive-backed verification).

content.title: How the CIS framework is structured
items: The CIS International Accreditation Evaluation Framework is organised in nine domains, lettered A to I. Domain I applies only to schools with boarding or homestay provision.

Verbatim from the Evaluation Framework: "This evaluation framework includes 8 domains, with 45 standards of which 24 are core standards. All core standards must be met or exceeded for a school to be accredited. If the school has boarding and/or homestay, there is a further domain including 8 standards, of which 5 are core."
Standards are designated either core or non-core. Meeting every core standard is a condition of accreditation; non-core standards support development rather than gate the decision.

The framework is underpinned by four drivers - how effectively a school delivers its own stated purpose and direction, provides effective student learning, ensures and enhances student well-being, and develops global citizenship.

Separately, the Process Overview describes Three Dimensions - Learning, Well-being and Guiding Principles - each with six aspirational standards, engaged during the self-study alongside the Cornerstones. The Three Dimensions do not replace Domains A to I; they are a second layer used for development, while the domains are where the evaluation happens.
For each domain the framework provides essential questions for reflection on the big picture of that domain, alongside the standards themselves.
Sources: CIS International Accreditation Evaluation Framework (Revised); Quick Guide to Standards; Process Overview v1.0, October 2024.

content.title: Correction note - what this section previously said
content.text: An earlier revision of this manual carried a warning that CIS had replaced its lettered domains with "18 standards across three dimensions" and that the domain letters were retired. That warning was wrong. The official CIS documents confirm the lettered domains A to I are current, and the Three Dimensions are a separate layer used during the self-study rather than a replacement. Domain references elsewhere in this manual that use the letters A to I are therefore correct in form; check only that the domain names match the official titles above, since some earlier tables used shortened or altered names.

content.title: CIS is changing its framework - what a school should plan against
content.text: Two CIS frameworks are in circulation, and they are not two descriptions of the same thing. The CIS International Accreditation Evaluation Framework [Revised] is the one this section maps to: 8 domains, 45 standards of which 24 are core, plus Domain I with a further 8 standards (5 core) for schools with boarding or homestay. It runs on a five-year cycle. CIS Instructions for Submission, updated August 2024, is addressed to "Schools Hosting Visits in 2025 using the CIS International Accreditation Framework", so this is the framework a school hosting a visit now is evaluated against. Separately, CIS International Accreditation NEW Evaluation Framework and Process Overview v1.0, dated October 2024, sets out a successor framework built on Three Dimensions and Cornerstones rather than lettered domains. That document was issued to early-adopter schools hosting Preparatory Engagement Visits in the first half of 2025 and states that published materials would follow at a public launch later that year. A school should therefore plan against the lettered domains and confirm with its CIS School Support and Evaluation Officer which framework its own visit will use. This manual will be re-mapped once the successor framework is published in full.

content.title: Best Practices for Evidence Management
steps: Collect Evidence Continuously Do not wait for accreditation self-study to begin collecting evidence. Embed evidence generation into daily workflows.
Organize as You Go File documents promptly in the correct EduNav folder with proper naming. Avoid accumulating unorganized files.
Version Control Matters When policies or documents are revised, archive old versions clearly labeled (e.g., "2024\Policy\Assessment\v1.0\Superseded.pdf") and mark the current version prominently.
Anonymize Sensitive Data For student or staff records shared with accreditation teams, remove identifying information (names, photos, ID numbers) while preserving the substance of evidence.
Quality Over Quantity Accreditation teams value concise, well-curated evidence more than exhaustive document dumps. Select representative samples that clearly demonstrate compliance.
Regular Backups EduNav should have automatic backups, but critical evidence should also be backed up locally (external drive, cloud storage) as redundancy.
Access Permissions Restrict sensitive evidence (HR files, safeguarding records, financial data) to authorized personnel only. Accreditation teams receive read-only access to relevant evidence.
Evidence Audit Schedule

items: Quarterly: Review one category of evidence (rotate through all categories over the year)
Annually: Comprehensive evidence audit of all categories
Pre-Self-Study: Intensive audit to identify and address gaps

This clause explains how a school runs its self-study: what it produces, who does the work, and in what order. A self-study is the school's own honest review of itself against the standards. It is not a document the school writes for the visiting team at the last minute. The visit checks what the self-study found.

content.title: The two processes are not the same shape
content.text: Eduversal partner schools work with two accreditors, and their self-study processes differ. Do not try to run one process and submit it twice. Plan them as two products drawn from one body of evidence.

content.title: Self-study at a glance — ACS WASC and CIS compared
rows: One self-study report in five chapters, produced by five Tasks (p.37)
A written reflection for each standard, with the school's own rating against the criteria
Leadership Team, Home Groups and Focus Groups (p.17)
The school decides. Most schools use a steering group plus a working group per domain
Strengths and growth needs per criterion
Four evaluation stages: Membership, Preparatory, Team, Future aspirations (p.2)
To the visiting committee no later than six weeks before the visit (p.14)
Submitted through the school's own digital space; date set with the CIS officers
Mid-cycle report in year three, with a possible one- or two-day review (p.15, p.31)
Progress is reviewed with the school's CIS officers across the five-year cycle

content.title: The five ACS WASC Tasks and what each produces
content.text: ACS WASC structures the self-study as five Tasks. Each Task produces one chapter of the report. The Model Timeline is at Focus on Learning 2019, p.37.

content.title: ACS WASC Tasks 1-5 and their products
rows: Summarise progress since the previous self-study
Chapter I: Progress Report on the schoolwide action plan
Refine the student and community profile from analysed data; clarify the schoolwide learner outcomes and the major student learner needs
Leadership Team or Profile Committee, with all stakeholders
Analyse the quality of the school programme against the ACS WASC criteria, focusing on the major student learner needs; decide strengths and growth needs
Summarise the identified major student learner needs from the profile and the group findings
Chapter IV: Summary of Identified Major Student Learner Needs
Revise the schoolwide action plan; set growth targets; set up follow-up monitoring
Leadership Team, with all stakeholders through Home and Focus Groups

content.title: A realistic timeline
items: Start about 18 months before the visit. Schools that start six months before produce a description of the school rather than an analysis of it, and visiting teams can tell the difference.
Months 1-3: the Principal names the coordinator and the groups, and the school agrees how it will collect evidence. Nothing is written yet.
Months 4-9: groups gather and analyse evidence. Most of the real work happens here.
Months 10-14: the school writes. Each group drafts its own part; the coordinator edits for one voice.
Months 15-16: the school agrees the action plan and checks that every claim in the report has evidence behind it.
At least six weeks before the visit: the ACS WASC report goes to the visiting committee (Focus on Learning 2019, p.14). Submit the CIS reflection on the date agreed with the CIS officers.

content.title: Quality tests to apply before you submit
items: Every judgement names its evidence. A statement with no evidence behind it is an opinion, and a visiting team will treat it as one.
The report says what is weak as well as what is strong. A self-study with no growth needs is not believed.
The findings and the action plan agree with each other. If Chapter III finds a problem, Chapter V must address it.
Staff who did not write the report recognise the school in it.
It is written in plain English. Most readers, including many staff, read English as an additional language.

Both accreditors expect the school community to take part in the self-study. Stakeholder involvement is part of the method, not an extra activity. A self-study written by three senior leaders is not a self-study, and both accreditors treat it as a weakness.

content.title: How ACS WASC organises participation
items: ACS WASC names three types of group (Focus on Learning 2019, p.17): the Leadership Team, Home Groups and Focus Groups.
Leadership Team: plans the process, keeps it moving, and edits the report so it reads as one document.
Home Groups: staff grouped by role or department. They analyse student data and achievement for their own area.
Focus Groups: mixed groups drawn from across the school. Each takes one criteria category (A to D) and analyses the whole school against it.
The two group types feed each other. Home Groups supply subject-level evidence; Focus Groups look across the school. A school that runs only one of the two produces a partial picture.

content.title: How CIS organises participation
items: CIS does not prescribe a group structure. The school chooses one and explains it.
Most schools use a steering group plus one working group per domain (A to H).
Each working group writes the reflection for its domain and gathers the evidence for it.
Domain I (Residential services) applies only to schools with boarding or homestay, so partner schools normally have eight working groups, not nine.

content.title: Who must be asked, and about what
items: Teaching staff — teaching and learning, curriculum, assessment, professional development, workload, and how supported they feel.
Support and administrative staff — systems, communication, and whether they can do their work well. They see problems teachers do not.
Students — whether they feel safe, known and challenged; whether they know how to improve; whether adults listen to them.
Parents — communication, reporting, and whether the school does what it says it does.
The Yayasan (foundation) and governors — direction, finance, and the school's long-term plan.
Alumni, where the school can reach them — how well the school prepared them for what came next.

content.title: Running surveys well
items: The Principal must decide, before the survey opens, what the school will do with the results. A survey the school does not act on damages trust more than no survey at all.
Offer surveys in Bahasa Indonesia as well as English. A parent answering in a second language gives you a shorter and less honest answer.
Keep responses anonymous, and say so clearly. Say who will see the results.
Ask a small number of clear questions. A long survey produces a low response rate and rushed answers at the end.
Report the results back to the people who answered, including the uncomfortable findings. This is the step schools skip, and it is the step that decides whether the next survey works.
Record the response rate for each group. A 12% parent response rate is itself a finding about communication.

This clause covers the practical preparation for an accreditation visit: what to send, what to give the team access to, and how to look after the school's data while doing it.

content.title: Before the visit — documents
items: ACS WASC: send the completed self-study report to the visiting committee members no later than six weeks before the visit (Focus on Learning 2019, p.14). This is a firm deadline. The team reads the report before they arrive.

CIS: submit the written reflections and the evidence in the school's own digital space, on the date agreed with the CIS officers. Evidence is never accepted by email (CIS Instructions for Submission, August 2024, p.8).
Send the school timetable, a site map, and the visit schedule with the report, so the team can plan their days.

content.title: Giving CIS access to evidence — the required set-up
items: Nominate one person to give IT support for file access during the visit, and share that contact with the final report (CIS Instructions for Submission, p.8).
Give read-only access to four parties: the School Services Advisor (SSA), the School Support and Evaluation Officer (SSEO), accreditation@cois.org, and the visiting evaluators (p.8).
Read-only means read-only. Links must not allow download, printing, or sharing onward (p.7).
Share with named individuals, never through a public link (p.7).
Share credentials safely — for example a one-time password that must be changed at first login. Do not send passwords or personal data by email (p.7).
Store financial documents separately, in their own password-protected location. Only the SSEO reviews them; volunteer evaluators do not need access unless the SSEO asks (p.7, p.8).
Remove access afterwards: volunteer evaluators two weeks after the visit ends, CIS accounts after the final report is published (p.8).

content.title: During the visit — practical arrangements
items: Give the team a private room with a door that closes, reliable internet, power sockets, and somewhere to leave papers safely overnight.
Do not put the team in a room where staff or students can overhear interviews.
Agree in advance who the team may talk to, and tell those people. Nobody should be surprised by an interview.
Let the team move around the school freely. A tightly controlled tour suggests the school is hiding something, even when it is not.
Name one person the team contacts with questions, and make sure that person is not teaching a full timetable that week.

content.title: What not to do
items: Do not rehearse students or staff. Visiting teams recognise it, and it costs the school credibility on everything else it says.
Do not repaint, redecorate or rearrange for the visit. The team is judging the normal school.
Do not hide a known weakness. A weakness the school has named and is acting on reads as strength; the same weakness found by the team reads as poor self-knowledge.

subsections.title: MINI SELF-REVIEWS AND CONTINUOUS ACCREDITATION READINESS

content.text: Accreditation runs on a cycle, not on a visit. Most of the cycle happens between visits. A school that stops working after a successful visit spends the next cycle rebuilding what it let go.

content.title: The ACS WASC six-year Cycle of Quality
rows: Update the profile, write a progress report, refine the schoolwide action plan
Update the profile, write a progress report, refine the action plan
Update the profile, write the mid-cycle progress report; a one- or two-day review is possible; refine the action plan
Update the profile, write a progress report, refine the action plan
Review all profile data, write a progress report, run the self-study process, refine the action plan
Complete the self-study, host the visit, refine the action plan — and the new cycle begins

content.title: The annual work between visits
items: Involve all stakeholders in reviewing progress (Focus on Learning 2019, p.31).
Summarise progress on each section of the schoolwide action plan every year, note the key evidence, and change the plan where it needs changing.
Review the schoolwide learner outcomes, the vision and the mission from time to time — not every year, but never once per cycle either.
Analyse data that shows whether the school is actually progressing, and write the mid-cycle report for ACS WASC in year three.
Be ready to host a one- or two-day review in year three if the school holds a six-year accreditation status (p.31).

content.title: Eduversal mini self-review — a light internal check
items: Once a year, and separately from the accreditor's requirements, each partner school should run a short internal review against two or three domains rather than all of them.
Rotate the domains so every domain is reviewed at least twice in a cycle.
Keep it to one working day. This is a health check, not a rehearsal of the self-study.
Use the same evidence the school already produces. If a review needs new documents created for it, it is testing paperwork rather than practice.
Send the result to the Academic Coordinator and the Principal, and record any action in the school improvement plan — not in a separate accreditation file that nobody opens.

The action plan is what the self-study is for. Everything before it — the data, the analysis, the findings — exists to produce a plan the school will actually follow.

content.title: One plan, not several
content.text: ACS WASC is explicit on this point: "The school integrates the school initiatives into one overall plan" (Focus on Learning 2019, p.69). A school must not keep an accreditation action plan beside a separate school improvement plan. Two plans compete for the same staff time, and the one nobody is watching is abandoned first. Merge them, and let the single plan serve both the accreditor and the school.

content.title: What each section of the plan must contain
items: A statement of the area for improvement, written in terms of students — what will be better for them, not what the school will install.
The reason for choosing it, taken from a specific self-study finding.
Growth targets for the whole school and for any subgroup that the data shows is behind.
The steps the school will take, in order.
Who is responsible for each step, by role.
The resources needed, including staff time.
How progress will be measured, and how often.
How the school will report progress to its stakeholders.

content.title: Writing targets that can be checked
items: Weak: "Improve student writing." Nobody can tell whether this happened.
Better: "Raise the proportion of Year 8 students reaching the expected standard in extended writing from 54% to 70% by June, measured by the common assessment."
A target must name the group, the measure, the starting point, the intended end point, and the date.
Three or four well-chosen targets beat twelve. A plan with twelve targets is a plan the school will not finish, and the visiting team knows this.

content.title: Keeping the plan alive between visits
items: The Principal must put the action plan on a leadership meeting agenda at a fixed interval — termly at least.
Each named owner reports on their own section. A plan reviewed only by the coordinator becomes the coordinator's plan.
Record what did not work and why. A plan that shows only successes is not being used honestly.
Update the plan when circumstances change. A plan that is never revised has stopped describing the school.

After an ACS WASC visit, the school should send the modified action plan to the ACS WASC office no later than six weeks after the visit, as one PDF or Word document, incorporating the areas for follow-up the visiting committee left (Focus on Learning 2019, p.137).

Evidence is the material that shows a claim is true. Both accreditors judge the school on evidence, not on description. This clause covers how to organise it so it can be found and used.

content.title: CIS rules for evidence files — these are requirements, not advice
items: Use a simple, logical naming convention. The filename must say what the file contains: "Teaching and Learning Policy", not "C1_Policy 4.23" (CIS Instructions for Submission, August 2024, p.5).

Do NOT put the standard or criteria number in the filename. One file is often hyperlinked from several parts of the report — a Teaching and Learning Policy may be cited under A2, C1 and D1 — and a number in the name makes it look as if it belongs to only one (p.5).
Hyperlink every piece of evidence from the writing that refers to it. A reader should never have to search for a file (p.5).
Store evidence somewhere searchable, and organise the folders so a stranger can navigate them (p.5).
Do not keep duplicate copies of the same file in different folders. Link to one copy.

content.title: What counts as strong evidence
content.text: Strong evidence shows practice, not intention. A policy shows what the school intends. A completed observation form, a set of minutes recording a decision, or a data set showing a change over time shows what the school does. Both are needed, but a folder holding only policies will not satisfy either accreditor.

content.title: Evidence types — with the Eduversal source for each
headers: Where it already exists at Eduversal
rows: Policy register, board minutes, organisational chart, Yayasan documents
Section 1 and Section 2; the policy register at 2.14
Schemes of work, curriculum maps, subject documentation
Section 5; the pacing documents each school maintains
Observation records, walkthrough notes, appraisal records, professional development logs
Section 7 and Section 12; the appraisal framework
Common assessment results, EASE data, Cambridge results analysis, reporting samples
Safeguarding policy, training records, incident logs, student voice records
Recruitment records, induction records, qualification register, staff composition data
Section 12; the SPK nationality composition at 12.2
Maintenance records, health and safety checks, risk assessments, IT and data protection records
Parent communication records, survey results, partnership agreements

content.title: Practical rules for the school
items: Collect evidence as it is produced, throughout the cycle. A school that assembles evidence in the final three months produces a thin file and exhausts its staff.
Name one person as evidence owner per domain — normally the person who already holds that work.
Check yearly that stored evidence is still current. Out-of-date evidence is worse than none: it shows the school is not looking.
Keep personal data out of shared evidence folders unless it is necessary, and follow Section 14 when it is. Accreditation does not suspend UU No. 27/2022.

Accreditation fails most often for one reason: everybody assumed somebody else was doing it. This clause names who does what. Each school writes the names of real people against these roles at the start of the cycle.

content.title: Roles inside the school
rows: Academic Coordinator, or a senior teacher given released time
Runs the process day to day. Keeps the timeline, chases drafts, edits the report into one voice, and is the single contact for the accreditors.
Owns the outcome. Decides the group structure. Protects the time the work needs. Approves the report before it is submitted, and answers to the Yayasan and to Eduversal for the result.
Principal, Accreditation Coordinator, Academic Coordinator, and domain or Focus Group leads
Meets regularly through the cycle. Reviews progress, resolves disagreements about findings, and signs off each chapter or reflection.
Lead the analysis for one domain or one criteria category, gather its evidence, and draft that part of the report.
Heads of department or phase leaders
Lead analysis of student data and achievement within their own area, and feed it to the Focus Groups.
The person who already produces that evidence
Keeps their domain's evidence current, named clearly, and hyperlinked from the report.
Provides access support for the evaluators' file access, and removes access on schedule after the visit. CIS requires this person to be nominated (CIS Instructions for Submission, August 2024, p.8).
Checks that sharing evidence with evaluators complies with UU No. 27/2022 and with Section 14.

content.title: External roles — who is who at the accreditor
rows: The school's operational contact for membership and submission matters.
Advises on the framework and the content of the reflections. The only person who reviews the school's financial documents (CIS Instructions for Submission, p.7).
The urgent support address. Also holds read-only access to the school's evidence space (p.8).
Read the reflections, visit the school, and report. Their access is removed two weeks after the visit ends (p.8).
Reads the self-study report at least six weeks before arriving. Visits the school. Leaves growth areas for the school to add to its action plan (Focus on Learning 2019, p.14, p.37).

content.title: Eduversal's role
items: Eduversal supports partner schools through the cycle. It does not run the self-study for them, and it must not: an accreditor judges the school's own capacity to see itself clearly.
The Subject Specialists and the Academic Board supply network-level evidence — the standards in this manual, the common assessment data, and the appraisal framework.
Eduversal reviews a school's draft report if asked, and gives an outside reading before submission.
A school must tell Eduversal when a visit is scheduled, so support can be planned around it.

content.title: Setting the roles at the start of the cycle
items: The Principal must fill these roles by name, in writing, before the self-study begins.
Give the Accreditation Coordinator released time. A coordinator with a full timetable will do the work badly and resent it.
Review the names each year. Staff leave, and an unowned role is discovered at the worst moment.

content.title: CONCLUSION — accreditation as embedded excellence
content.text: Accreditation is not a destination—it is a journey of continuous improvement. By embedding accreditation practices into our daily operations through: ✓ Systematic evidence collection (Section 18.4) ✓ Comprehensive crosswalks linking practice to standards (Section 18.3) ✓ Meaningful stakeholder engagement (Section 18.6) ✓ Rigorous self-study (Section 18.5) ✓ Thorough visit preparation (Section 18.7) ✓ Termly mini self-reviews (Section 18.8) ✓ Action-oriented improvement cycles (Section 18.9) ...we ensure that accreditation becomes a natural validation of our commitment to excellence, not an overwhelming compliance burden. Eduversal Partner Schools pursue CIS and WASC accreditation because we believe in:

items: Transparent accountability to our students, parents, and community
Evidence-based decision-making driven by data and stakeholder feedback
Continuous reflection and improvement in service of student learning and wellbeing
International recognition that opens doors for our students globally

content.text: When accreditation is embedded in how we work—when evidence generation is part of professional practice, when stakeholder feedback is routinely sought, when improvement is systematic—then accreditation becomes what it should be: a celebration of quality, not a test to pass. This toolkit is intended to help Eduversal Partner School Principals and leadership teams lead accreditation with confidence, clarity, and purpose. Use it well, and accreditation will strengthen everything we do in service of our mission and our students' success.
